processing: Very lightly oxidised (roughly 10–20%), carefully ball-rolled and gently dried with no roast, so the cup is about the slow-grown leaf rather than the craft.
harvest_season: Usually only two harvests because of the altitude: a late-spring crop picked from late May into June and a winter crop in October; the highest gardens may give a single pick in some years.
appearance_dry: Large, tightly rolled dark jade balls with a waxy sheen, noticeably heavy for their size.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold with a green tint, thick-looking and perfectly clear.
appearance_wet: Big, thick, almost leathery whole leaves, deep green with a faint red edge, on sturdy stems.
taste_profile: Dense, cold sweetness like pear and white flowers over an oily, almost syrupy body, with very little bitterness and a cooling aftertaste that keeps returning for minutes.

brewing.notes: Easy to under-leaf: use a full dose and boiling water, and let the balls open fully in the first steep. Tolerates long steeps better than Alishan and rewards patience over eight or more infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest and sub-area: the late-spring (June) and winter (October) picks of the current year, usually in vacuum-sealed 75 g or 150 g packs, and priced by altitude with Hua Gang, Cui Luan and Fushoushan lots at the top. Winter lots are often considered thicker and spring lots more aromatic; both are meant to be drunk within a year and are not aged.
description:
Li Shan, 'Pear Mountain', is the collective name for the high-altitude tea gardens around the village of Lishan in Heping District, Taichung, strung along the Central Cross-Island Highway at roughly 1,800 to 2,500 metres among apple, pear and peach orchards. Together with Da Yu Ling it sits at the top of Taiwan's high-mountain hierarchy, and the sub-areas, Hua Gang, Cui Luan, Wuling, Fushoushan, Tianfu and Songmao, are often named on the packet because buyers pay by altitude.

The cultivar is almost always Qing Xin oolong. At this height the bushes grow slowly through cold nights and thin air, which builds thick, waxy leaves rich in amino acids and sugars; the makers do as little as possible to them, a very light oxidation, careful ball-rolling and a gentle drying with no roast, so the cup is about the leaf, not the processing.

What you get is weight and cold sweetness: a dense, oily liquor that feels almost as if it had sugar in it, with pear, white flowers and cool mountain air rather than the loud florals of lower tea, and an aftertaste that keeps returning for minutes. It is easy to under-leaf. Use a proper dose, water right off the boil, and give the balls a slightly longer first steep to open; the tea tolerates long steeps better than Alishan does and rewards patience over eight or more infusions.

Because of the altitude there are usually only two harvests, a late spring crop picked from late May into June and a winter crop in October, and both are expensive; the highest sub-areas may give only one pick a year. The name is heavily faked, so a specific garden or sub-area, a harvest date and a vacuum-sealed pack from a seller who can say which farm the tea came from matter more than the words 'Li Shan' on the label.

Drink it within a year while the cold, sweet character is fresh; it does not improve with time. Brew it alone and with attention; this is a tea that gets lost next to food.
